How I got here

The short version: I learned engineering on systems that weren't allowed to fail. Now I want to help teams decide what to build in the first place.

I studied Electronics and Telecommunications Engineering at KS Institute of Technology in Bangalore and started my career at DXC Technology in 2021, on a z/OS batch system that processed membership and claims data for Blue Cross Blue Shield. Early on, the two senior engineers on the account left, and another new hire and I took over the system between us.

That stretch shaped how I work. When a nightly job fails, fixing it is only the first question. The next ones are which downstream reports are now wrong, who will act on them, and how to stop it from happening again. I learned to read logs closely, validate data end to end, and write the monitoring that catches the next failure before it turns into an escalation. Later I trained the engineers who joined after me.

I came to Rutgers for an MS in Computer Science to get closer to the questions that sit above the system: what it should do, what it should cost, and whether it is worth building at all. The program gave me a technical toolkit in machine learning and modeling, and my main project now is an LLM pipeline that reads SEC filings. I kept one production habit throughout: I write down where an analysis falls short, because that was always the most useful part of any incident report.

The work I enjoy most sits where technology meets a business decision. I built a five-year model for whether companies should rent or own their compute, and I wrote a position paper on why large cloud users may move back to private infrastructure. That is why I'm focused on strategy, solutions, and consulting: helping a team frame the problem, test the options with real numbers, and explain the trade-offs to the people who decide. AI/ML is one of the tools I bring to that work, not the whole job.

Lead project

Rent vs. Own: Cloud Cost Decision Framework

Rutgers, team of fiveMarch to April 2026

  • Cost modeling
  • Sensitivity analysis
  • AWS pricing

A five-year model comparing AWS reserved and on-demand compute against owned co-located hardware for Shopify (about 20 baseline instances) and Netflix's origin tier (about 2,400), under stable, spiky, and high-growth workloads. I led the Shopify case study: estimating baseline instance counts from public revenue and throughput data, then modeling hardware amortization against operating cost. The end product is a decision framework that maps workload type to deployment choice.

What held up

Workload shape, not company size, decided the answer. The break-even hardware cost came out near $12.2K per server in both cases despite a 100× difference in scale, because it depends on per-instance economics. A sensitivity analysis on six parameters left the scenario winners unchanged, including ±20% cloud pricing and +30% hardware cost.

What I logged

Staffing costs are excluded from the base model, and the conclusions assume refurbished hardware. At new-hardware prices of $15K or more per server, owning stops beating reserved cloud.

Financial Filing Analysis Agent

Personal project2026, in progress

  • Python
  • Claude API
  • SEC EDGAR
  • Pydantic

A pipeline that pulls 10-K filings from EDGAR, isolates the Risk Factors and MD&A sections, and uses Claude to extract sentiment, forward guidance, and risk signals into a fixed schema validated with Pydantic. I built it because filings are where companies say the most and get read the least, and I wanted to see how much of that an LLM could pull out reliably.

What held up

Runs end to end across six companies in tech, e-commerce, banking, and retail (Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Bank of America, Walmart, Target), after fixing section-parsing bugs caused by false table-of-contents matches and inconsistent character encoding.

What I logged

Some large banks incorporate MD&A by reference to a separate annual report rather than the 10-K itself. I recorded this as a scope limitation, not a bug, and it now shapes which companies the pipeline targets.

Next: a hand-labeled evaluation set to measure extraction accuracy against ground truth, and quarter-over-quarter signal comparison.

Incentive-Compatible Rewards for Confidence Reporting

Rutgers, team of fourMechanism design and RL

  • Q-learning
  • Contextual bandits
  • Reward design
  • Calibration

A helper-bot agent chooses between a fast answer and an accurate one across easy, hard, and ambiguous queries, then reports its confidence. We compared four reward designs to see which ones produce agents that are both useful and honest about uncertainty.

What held up

A speed-only reward produced textbook specification gaming: the agent chose Fast almost every time, whatever the query. A balanced reward gave a sensible context-dependent policy. Penalizing confidence reports that didn't match the agent's own softmax-derived belief pushed honesty close to 100% and raised accuracy on ambiguous queries.

What I logged

The environment is static, with fixed accuracy probabilities. Real task distributions drift, and an agent would need to update both its beliefs and its reporting strategy as they do.

Structural Analysis of the Spotify Tracks Dataset

RutgersMarch to May 2026

  • PCA
  • t-SNE
  • UMAP
  • GMM
  • VAE

An unsupervised study of about 114,000 songs across 114 genres to find which of ten audio features carry musical signal and which are noise, followed by a 3D variational autoencoder in PyTorch to generate synthetic tracks.

What held up

PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP independently pointed to the same dominant “intensity” axis, built from energy, loudness, and acousticness. Generated output was checked with KS statistics and cluster analysis.

What I logged

Partial mode collapse in the VAE: rarer song types were underrepresented in generated output.

Brain Tumor Segmentation with U-Net

Rutgers, team of fourWork shared equally across the teamMachine learning course

  • PyTorch
  • U-Net
  • BraTS 2020
  • Medical imaging

Multi-class segmentation of tumor sub-regions (necrotic core, edema, enhancing tumor) from 369 BraTS 2020 patient volumes. All four MRI modalities (T1, T1CE, T2, FLAIR) are z-score normalized per modality and stacked as input channels over 57,000+ 2D slices. The model is trained with a combined Dice and cross-entropy loss, with early stopping on validation Dice.

What held up

Validation Dice stabilized around 0.88 against about 0.91 on training, a small gap. Predicted masks matched ground truth in shape and boundary on held-out slices.

What I logged

The model segments one 2D slice at a time, so it can't use context from neighboring slices of the same scan. A 3D or 2.5D input is the natural next step.

Autonomous Agents Under Uncertainty

Rutgers CS520, three projectsFebruary to May 2025

  • A* variants
  • Bayesian inference
  • CNN
  • Simulation

Three connected problems on a spaceship grid, all about the same question: how should an agent act when it can't see the whole picture?

  • Fire spread. Four path-planning bots navigating a spreading fire. A risk-aware bot that adds fire-spread probability to Adaptive A* path costs outperformed plain and repeated A*, especially at high flammability, over 200 trials per setting. Code
  • Space rat tracking. Bayesian belief updates over every open cell from a noisy distance sensor, plus a diffusion step once the rat moves. My redesigned search bot won about 95% of runs with low sensor sensitivity. The simpler baseline overtook it as sensitivity rose, and I kept that result in the report. Code
  • Localization. A CNN trained on 47,570 simulated belief states from 200 mazes predicts how many moves localization will take. That estimate drives one-step lookahead policies, which gave modest improvements over the rule-based baseline on larger belief sets. Code

Writing

A position paper, written to argue one side and answer the other.

The Erosion of Cloud Trust: Why Large-Scale Users Will Return to Private Infrastructure

Position paper, March 2026

The paper argues that three pressures on trust in the public cloud will push large organizations toward private, hybrid, and multi-cloud setups: rising security incidents driven by misconfiguration, lock-in built into pricing and egress fees, and outages whose blast radius spans thousands of tenants. It takes the strongest case for public cloud seriously before answering it, drawing on repatriation cases such as 37signals, Dropbox, and GEICO, and on the October 2025 AWS US-EAST-1 outage.
